title: Quarry for docs
text:
Building a corpus-wide DataFrame
from udsyntax import load_latin, SyntaxGraph, corpus_to_polars

nlp = load_latin()
graphs = [SyntaxGraph.from_doc(nlp(text), urn=urn) for urn, text in lines]
corpus_df = corpus_to_polars(graphs)
When a graph’s urn is a parseable CTS URN (urn:cts:namespace:group.work.version:passage), corpus_to_polars adds group / work / version / passage columns automatically.

title: Quick start
text:
After doing a normal spaCy analysis with nlp, you can create a SyntaxGraph from the result:
from udsyntax import load_latin, SyntaxGraph

nlp = load_latin()  # loads la_core_web_lg, cached after the first call
doc = nlp("Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres.")

graph = SyntaxGraph.from_doc(doc)
df = graph.to_polars()   # one row per token
g = graph.to_networkx()  # requires the `graph` extra

title: Loading a CEX corpus
text:
CEX files are urn|text lines, one per citable passage. read_cex can filter by a substring of the URN to preselect particular works.
from udsyntax import read_cex

lines = read_cex("genesis.cex", urn_filter="vulgate")
urns = [urn for urn, _ in lines]
texts = [text for _, text in lines]

title: Visualizing a graph
text:
udsyntax includes Python functions and utility scripts to create diagrams of SyntaxGraphs.



udsyntax and the spaCy pipeline for whichever --lang you pass, already installed
local install of graphviz to render a png file

Install dot:
Mac OS:
brew install graphviz
Windows: download from https://graphviz.org/download/ or
winget install --id Graphviz.Graphviz
Verify it worked: print a version string.
dot -V



text_to_dot.py: analyze and graph a string
python scripts/text_to_dot.py "Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres." --lang la | dot -Tpng -o bg_1_1.png
corpus_to_dot.py: identify a passage by URN, analyze it, generate its dot representation
python3 scripts/corpus_to_dot.py scratch/data/compnov.cex --urn "urn:cts:compnov:bible.genesis.vulgate:1.1" --lang la | dot -Tpng -o genesis_1_1.png
Parameters:

corpus (positional, one or more): CEX files (urn|text lines) to search, read and concatenated in the order given via udsyntax.read_cex_many.
--urn (required): the exact URN of the passage to select (via the new udsyntax.select_urn, an exact match, not the substring urn_filter that read_cex/read_cex_many accept). If more than one line across the given files shares this URN, a warning goes to stderr and the first one is used. If none matches, the script exits with an error naming the URN and the files searched.
--lang / -l (required): la for Latin (la_core_web_lg) or grc for Ancient Greek (grc_dep_web_lg).

title: Visualizing a graph
text:
Composing diagrams from Python
udsyntax includes two functions, to_mermaid() and to_dot(), that diagram a SyntaxGraph using the syntax of Mermaid or the open-source graphviz package.
graph = SyntaxGraph.from_doc(doc)

print(graph.to_mermaid())                  # "graph BT" ... (root-at-top tree)
print(graph.to_mermaid(orientation="LR"))  # left-to-right instead

print(graph.to_dot())                      # a Graphviz "digraph { ... }"
print(graph.to_dot(orientation="LR"))      # left-to-right instead

title: Installing uvsytax
text:
Install the package from its GitHub repository:
pip install git+https://github.com/neelsmith/udsyntax.git
You’ll also need a spaCy pipeline for whichever language you’re parsing:
pip install "la-core-web-lg @ https://huggingface.co/latincy/la_core_web_lg/resolve/main/la_core_web_lg-3.9.6-py3-none-any.whl"
pip install "grc-dep-web-lg @ https://huggingface.co/latincy/grc_dep_web_lg/resolve/main/grc_dep_web_lg-3.8.1-py3-none-any.whl"
If you want to export graphs to networkx, install the graph extra:
pip install "udsyntax[graph] @ git+https://github.com/neelsmith/udsyntax.git"
